finding-bottlenecks.body: Client traces show rapid setup and upload followed by a long first-byte wait. Server traces locate most of that interval in a database queue. Increasing network capacity cannot remove the queue. Bound downstream concurrency, investigate service time, and validate the effect on end-to-end percentiles. Keep checking for bottleneck migration after a fix instead of assuming one successful optimization solves every load level.

fallacies-of-distributed-computing.title: Replace optimistic assumptions with explicit limits
fallacies-of-distributed-computing.body: Networks can fail, have nonzero latency, finite bandwidth, changing topology, multiple administrators, nonzero cost, heterogeneous components, and security threats. These are design constraints rather than reasons to avoid distribution entirely. Each remote boundary needs defined timeouts, failure handling, compatibility, and ownership. Local function-call intuition fails when a caller cannot immediately know whether the remote side completed an action.

fallacies-of-distributed-computing.title: Example: moving a helper into a service
fallacies-of-distributed-computing.body: A helper previously returned in memory with ordinary exceptions. After becoming remote, calls can arrive late, be duplicated by recovery, or complete while the caller times out. Add an operation contract covering deadlines, idempotency, and observability. Serializing the old function arguments over HTTP is only the transport step; it does not automatically preserve the original failure semantics.

failure-modes-and-partitions.title: Failure is often partial and ambiguous
failure-modes-and-partitions.body: A timeout means an expected result did not arrive within a budget. The request might never have arrived, might still be running, or might have committed with its response lost. A partition can prevent selected participants from communicating while others continue. Detection is based on delayed observations, so a slow service and an unreachable service can initially look similar.

failure-modes-and-partitions.title: Example: payment response lost
failure-modes-and-partitions.body: The server commits a payment, then the return path fails. The client cannot safely infer failure and issue a new independent payment. Use a stable operation identifier and a way to retrieve the established outcome. Increasing the timeout changes the observation window but cannot eliminate ambiguity under every failure. Recovery must be designed around the operation's meaning, not only transport exceptions.

retries-and-backoff.title: Recovery consumes capacity too
retries-and-backoff.body: Retries can hide transient failures but amplify overload. Bound attempts by a total deadline and retry budget, use backoff with jitter where appropriate, and retry only operations whose semantics permit it. Several retrying layers can multiply attempts unexpectedly. A downstream overload signal should influence admission rather than causing every caller to immediately repeat the same failed work.

retries-and-backoff.title: Worked amplification
retries-and-backoff.body: A client makes up to three attempts and a gateway independently makes up to three downstream attempts per incoming call. One user operation can generate nine downstream attempts. Four similarly configured layers could generate far more. Place retries deliberately, carry deadlines, and record attempt counts. Jitter spreads retry timing but does not reduce the total work unless budgets and admission rules also constrain it.

idempotency.title: Deduplicate an operation, not just a packet
idempotency.body: An idempotency key identifies one logical operation across retries. The server needs a defined scope, payload-consistency rule, retention period, and concurrent-request behavior. Recording the key separately from the operation without atomic coordination can still permit duplicates or lost results. Transport sequence numbers do not provide this application-level guarantee across new requests and connections.

idempotency.title: Example: two simultaneous creates
idempotency.body: Two requests with the same key arrive together. A safe design prevents both from independently performing the side effect and returns the established outcome according to policy. If the same key is reused with a different payload, reject or otherwise handle the conflict explicitly. Expiration matters: retrying after the deduplication record has disappeared may no longer have the same protection.

circuit-breakers.title: Stop repeatedly calling a failing dependency
circuit-breakers.body: A circuit breaker observes failures and can temporarily reject calls while a dependency appears unhealthy. A half-open phase permits limited probes before broader traffic resumes. This is distinct from a timeout, retry policy, and bulkhead limit, though they interact. Incorrect thresholds or shared state can block healthy traffic or reopen into another overload burst.

circuit-breakers.title: Example: recovery under a flood
circuit-breakers.body: A dependency returns after an outage, but thousands of waiting callers immediately retry. A breaker with controlled probes and bounded admission can make recovery less abrupt. Decide whether rejection has a safe fallback and expose breaker state in telemetry. Returning cached data may be acceptable for a catalog but inappropriate for an operation requiring current authoritative account state.

load-balancing-l4-l7.title: Different layers expose different routing choices
load-balancing-l4-l7.body: Layer-4 balancing makes decisions using transport-related information, while layer-7 balancing can inspect application metadata such as HTTP hostnames and paths when it terminates or otherwise understands the protocol. Connection persistence, multiplexing, affinity, and health policy influence distribution. Equal connection counts do not guarantee equal work when some connections carry far more requests than others.

load-balancing-l4-l7.title: Example: a few heavy multiplexed connections
load-balancing-l4-l7.body: An L4 balancer assigns long-lived connections evenly, but one carries thousands of expensive streams while another is nearly idle. Backend load becomes uneven despite equal connection counts. Application-aware balancing may offer different choices, with added termination and operational responsibilities. Measure request cost, active work, and connection lifetime before blaming randomness or adding servers without changing the distribution problem.

health-checks-and-discovery.title: Reachability, readiness, and usefulness differ
health-checks-and-discovery.body: A process can be alive but unable to serve requests; a port can accept connections while every backend call fails. Health checks should reflect the intended routing decision without causing cascading removals under transient dependency failures. Service discovery publishes endpoints, but clients may cache them. Membership changes and health decisions therefore need bounded propagation and safe handling of stale endpoints.

health-checks-and-discovery.title: Example: a new instance warms up
health-checks-and-discovery.body: A process starts listening before loading required data. Marking it ready immediately routes requests into predictable failures. Gate readiness on the minimum required serving state while keeping liveness focused on recoverable process health. During deployment, account for discovery caches and active connections; removing an endpoint from one registry does not instantly stop all clients from using it.

graceful-shutdown.title: Stop admission before destroying active work
graceful-shutdown.body: Graceful shutdown separates refusing new work, draining existing operations, notifying peers where the protocol allows, and closing after a bounded deadline. Listener closure, discovery removal, and active-connection handling are different steps. A process should not wait forever for a client that never finishes, but forced termination can leave ambiguous outcomes that retry logic must still handle.

graceful-shutdown.title: Example: deploying behind a load balancer
graceful-shutdown.body: Mark an instance unavailable for new routing, allow propagation, stop accepting new requests appropriately, and finish bounded in-flight work. Multiplexed protocols may need explicit shutdown signaling rather than closing every connection immediately. Preserve a maximum drain period and observe unfinished requests. A successful deployment script does not prove every old request completed without interruption.

backpressure-and-rate-limiting.title: Control outstanding work and arrival rate
backpressure-and-rate-limiting.body: Backpressure reacts to downstream capacity; rate limiting constrains admission over time. Concurrency limits cap simultaneous operations, while token buckets permit controlled bursts under a long-run rate. Queues must be bounded and have meaningful expiration. Applying one limit at a single layer does not protect every resource, especially when one admitted request triggers substantial fan-out.

backpressure-and-rate-limiting.title: Worked queue example
backpressure-and-rate-limiting.body: Arrivals at 150 requests per second and service at 100 create 50 queued requests per second in a constant-rate model. A 500-request buffer fills in ten seconds. Doubling it postpones rejection but increases possible waiting without changing sustainable capacity. Reject, slow producers, or increase effective service according to semantics, and monitor oldest-request age rather than relying solely on queue length.

tls-deep-dive.title: Channel protection has defined boundaries
tls-deep-dive.body: TLS protects application traffic between its endpoints, with peer authentication according to configuration. Symmetric traffic keys protect records after establishment, and handshake integrity binds the negotiated session. Terminating TLS at a proxy creates a new trust boundary; a separate backend connection needs its own required protection. Encryption does not fix authorization mistakes or unsafe behavior after decryption.

tls-deep-dive.title: Example: two encrypted segments
tls-deep-dive.body: A browser connects securely to an edge proxy, which connects securely to an origin. The proxy can access plaintext because it is an endpoint of both sessions. This may be intentional, but it is not one end-to-end opaque channel from browser to origin. Document who can decrypt, how peers are authenticated, and where logs or traces may expose decrypted application data.

certificate-validation.title: Verify identity as well as cryptography
certificate-validation.body: Certificate validation checks an acceptable trust path, intended service identity, validity period, and relevant constraints and policy. Clock errors, missing intermediates, wrong hostnames, or inconsistent deployment can cause failures. A certificate accepted for one hostname is not necessarily acceptable for another. Disabling verification changes the security property rather than fixing the original deployment problem.

certificate-validation.title: Example: only some clients fail
certificate-validation.body: One client has a cached intermediate or a different trust store while another does not. A server can also present different certificates based on name indication or load-balanced instance. Compare the actual handshake and served chain, not just a certificate file on one machine. Reproduce using the intended hostname and a clean trust context before concluding the network path is broken.

mitm-replay-downgrade.title: Different attacks exploit different assumptions
mitm-replay-downgrade.body: A man-in-the-middle attack interferes between peers; replay repeats previously valid material; downgrade attempts push peers toward weaker behavior. Authenticated encryption and negotiation protections address parts of this problem, while application freshness and authorization address others. A valid encrypted message can still be inappropriate to execute twice if the application does not bind it to a unique, current operation.

mitm-replay-downgrade.title: Example: replay-sensitive early actions
mitm-replay-downgrade.body: An application receives an operation through a mode where replay risk must be considered. Restrict early actions to suitable semantics or enforce explicit anti-replay and operation identity controls. Do not assume encryption alone provides freshness for every application command. Also avoid silent fallback to weaker verification after errors; attackers may deliberately trigger the error path that changes the policy.

ddos.title: Exhaustion can target different resources
ddos.body: SYN floods stress connection-establishment handling; amplification abuses services that send large replies to spoofed requests; slow-client attacks retain application resources with little traffic. Defenses must match the constrained resource, including upstream capacity, connection state, parsing work, and worker occupancy. Host-only limits cannot restore a saturated access link before traffic reaches the host.

ddos.title: Example: low bandwidth, high impact
ddos.body: A small number of clients slowly send incomplete requests and occupy all workers. Traffic volume stays modest while legitimate users cannot progress. Progress deadlines, bounded headers and bodies, admission controls, and suitable connection handling address this path. A bandwidth threshold alone misses it. Validate mitigations against legitimate slow clients so availability protection does not indiscriminately reject normal usage.

dns-spoofing.title: False naming data redirects later trust decisions
dns-spoofing.body: DNS spoofing and cache poisoning try to make clients or resolvers accept incorrect naming information. Query matching, resolver hardening, and DNSSEC validation address different parts of answer integrity. Encrypted DNS protects a transport segment but is not the same as signed-data validation. HTTPS identity checks provide another boundary even when an attacker influences a resolved address.

dns-spoofing.title: Example: an answer points to the wrong server
dns-spoofing.body: A client receives an attacker-selected address for a legitimate hostname. If TLS identity validation remains correct, the attacker still needs an acceptable identity for that hostname to impersonate the HTTPS service. If verification is disabled, that additional protection disappears. Layer defenses deliberately, and investigate authoritative changes, resolver caches, and local overrides before assuming every unexpected answer is poisoning.

firewalls-and-ids.title: Enforcement and detection have different jobs
firewalls-and-ids.body: A firewall permits or rejects traffic according to policy, often with connection-state tracking. Intrusion detection observes suspicious behavior; prevention systems can actively block selected patterns. Neither automatically understands every encrypted application action. Rules need an explicit trust model, correct placement, logging, and testing. A successful packet match does not establish application authorization or prove benign intent.

firewalls-and-ids.title: Example: a permitted port carries unwanted actions
firewalls-and-ids.body: Allowing HTTPS to a service admits encrypted transport on the selected path, not every possible operation safely. The application must still authenticate users and authorize requests. Conversely an IDS alert is evidence requiring interpretation, not proof of compromise. Test allowed and denied paths in both directions and account for NAT and proxy boundaries that change the addresses visible to each control.

vpn-protocols.title: The tunnel is one part of a trust design
vpn-protocols.body: IPsec, WireGuard, and OpenVPN provide different mechanisms and operational models for protected tunnels. Key distribution, peer identity, routing, endpoint policy, and renewal matter as much as encryption choice. Tunnel overhead changes effective packet size, and full-tunnel versus split-tunnel routing changes which traffic traverses the VPN. Being connected does not imply unrestricted authorization to every internal service.

vpn-protocols.title: Example: small traffic works, large traffic stalls
vpn-protocols.body: A VPN establishes successfully and small requests succeed, but large transfers fail because encapsulation reduces usable MTU and required size feedback is unavailable. Investigate packet size and path handling rather than replacing credentials repeatedly. Also verify DNS and routes supplied to clients. A working encrypted tunnel can coexist with an incorrect internal route or application access denial.

zero-trust.title: Do not equate network location with authority
zero-trust.body: Zero-trust designs evaluate access using identity, device or workload context, and resource-specific policy rather than granting broad trust solely from being on an internal network. It is an architectural approach, not one product or the absence of firewalls. Authentication, least privilege, segmentation, credential lifecycle, and monitoring need consistent enforcement across user and service interactions.

zero-trust.title: Example: a compromised internal workload
zero-trust.body: A workload with valid network reachability should still be unable to call unrelated administrative APIs without the required identity and permission. Short-lived credentials and narrow authorization reduce the usefulness of stolen access, but require reliable issuance and revocation behavior. Test denied operations as well as successful ones; adding an identity proxy without removing bypass paths leaves the original trust gap intact.
